card.hook: Jemaa el-Fnaa never sits still. Juice sellers, musicians and performers fill the day, then the food stalls light up once it gets dark. It's a lot to fit in one photo, so go up high.
card.stand_here: Go up to the rooftop terrace of Le Grand Balcon du Café Glacier. You reach it through the ground-floor café, and it's worth asking there which side of the square it's on. Face the square, with the Koutoubia minaret behind it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the whole square. Try 0.5x if you want more crowd and stalls in the frame. Then zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a single stall, a performer or a glowing food stand without leaning over the edge.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and keep your phone level so the buildings don't lean. Then tap the bright sky or the minaret and slide the picture a little darker so the sunset colours stay rich.
card.best_time: Go for sunset, and get there early because the terrace fills up. You can shoot the daytime square and the lit-up evening square from the same spot. After dark, switch on night mode and rest your elbows on the rail to keep the picture sharp.
card.selfie_here: Try the third-floor open-air terrace of the Café de France on the west side of the square. Guides describe a wide view over the whole square with the Koutoubia minaret in sight. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x to fit more in, and keep the minaret over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Watch for pickpockets in dense crowds on the square. At street level, ask before photographing people. Photo-prop monkeys and snake charmers charge per shot.
card.challenge: Take the same corner of the square twice, once at sunset and once after dark, and see which one you'd frame.
card.good_to_know: Marrakech was founded in 1070, and the square began as an open market space next to a fortress. In 2008 UNESCO added it to its List of Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, which recognises its living traditions rather than its buildings. A major renovation began in May 2025, so it may look different from older photos.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Go up to the rooftop terrace of Le Grand Balcon du Café Glacier. You reach it through the ground-floor café, and it's worth asking there which side of the square it's on. Face the square, with the Koutoubia minaret behind it.

card.hook: Picture a blue house so bold it looks painted on the sky, sitting perfectly upside down in a pond. Get there early and the water plays along.
card.stand_here: Head to Jardin Majorelle's central lily pond and stand at the phone icon on the map, about 160 m south of the subject, facing north. You'll be looking across the water at the blue villa, with papyrus on both sides and blue pots in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the villa and its reflection. Try 0.5x at the lily basin so the water and palms fit together, and 2x or more to pick out the blue pots, cacti or a single papyrus frame (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Tap the villa, then slide the brightness a touch darker so the blue stays rich instead of washed out.
card.best_time: Go at opening, around 8am, when the water is calm and the reflection is clearest. Opening hours change with the season, so check the official site before you go.
card.selfie_here: Try the small square off the sloping cross-path just before the Blue Villa, where cacti sit in front of the blue facade. It's a great villa view rather than a known selfie spot, so use the front camera (0.5x if your phone has it) and turn until that blue wall lands over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography isn't allowed inside the museums, so keep your phone for the grounds. Entry is timed and tickets are sold online, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Hold your phone low, just above the blue pots, and see if you can fit the pot, the pond and the villa into one shot.
card.good_to_know: French painter Jacques Majorelle began the garden in 1923 and worked on it for almost forty years. The deep blue he used is now called Majorelle Blue. Yves Saint Laurent and Pierre Bergé rescued it in the 1980s, and the Cubist villa, designed by Paul Sinoir, now houses the Berber Museum.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to Jardin Majorelle's central lily pond and stand at the phone icon on the map, about 160 m south of the subject, facing north. You'll be looking across the water at the blue villa, with papyrus on both sides and blue pots in front of you.

card.hook: Picture a palm-lined path with a grand hotel closing the scene at the far end. That's the quiet, green side of La Mamounia, and it looks nothing like the fancy interiors you've seen online.
card.stand_here: Stand in Jardins de La Mamounia, the garden area behind the hotel building. The hotel lies to the north-west, so face that way and look across the open lawns and palm-lined paths towards its rear buildings.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the lawn, path and hotel in one picture. Go to 0.5x for more garden, or 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the building between the palms.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, line a garden path up with one of the vertical lines, and keep a few palms in the foreground for depth.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or late in the afternoon, when the light is softer and the lawns and walls look warmer. At midday the palm shade and bright walls make the contrast harsh.
card.selfie_here: The classic selfie spot is the black-and-white columned hall inside the hotel, where the high-contrast columns frame you nicely. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep a column or two behind you. It's not a free public spot, though, so don't count on getting in.
card.rules_and_safety: The gardens belong to a hotel, so check at the entrance on Avenue Bab Jdid whether you can walk in. You may also need to ask permission before entering the open-air marble corridor.
card.challenge: Keep the phone level so every palm trunk stands up straight, then see if you can get a path to lead the eye right to the hotel.
card.good_to_know: La Mamounia opened in 1929, designed by Henri Prost and Antoine Marchisio, and it mixes Moroccan architecture with Art Deco. It stands on a palace and garden that Sultan Mohammed ben Abdallah gave to his son, Moulay Mamoun, in the 18th century. The garden still covers about 8.1 hectares, so you have plenty of room to try different angles.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Jardins de La Mamounia, the garden area behind the hotel building. The hotel lies to the north-west, so face that way and look across the open lawns and palm-lined paths towards its rear buildings.

selfie_spots.why: Several guides rank this corridor as the hotel's most photographed interior, and its high-contrast columns frame a visitor well, especially in a flowy dress.

card.hook: Picture a huge, flat mirror of water with olive trees around it and a tidy two-storey pavilion sitting on the edge, like it's waiting for its portrait. That's Menara Gardens, and it's an easy one to get right.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 80 m south-east of the pavilion and basin, and face north-west. The High Atlas mountains are behind you from here, so they won't be in your shot.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole basin and pavilion together. Try 0.5x down low for more water and sky, then 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the pavilion's arches and balcony.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the water's edge on a lower line, then tap the pavilion and slide a bit darker so the bright sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Pick a clear day, ideally morning or late afternoon, when the sun is lower and the sky is softer. Clear days also give you the best chance of spotting the mountains in the distance.
card.selfie_here: Switch to the front camera, try 0.5x, and turn your back to the pavilion so it sits over your shoulder with the water below. Glance at the screen to check the pavilion is really in the frame before you smile.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the water's edge on the side of the basin across from the pavilion, so they can shoot you with the water in the foreground.
card.rules_and_safety: The pavilion's upper balcony is reached by a narrow, steep staircase, which may be hard if you have limited mobility. Access rules and any entry charge can change, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get one shot where the pavilion's reflection sits in the water and the water's edge lines up with the lower gridline. Bonus points if it looks like two pavilions.
card.good_to_know: The basin is about 195 metres long and 160 metres wide. The gardens were first laid out around 1157 under the Almohad ruler Abd al-Mu'min, and the pavilion you see now was completed in 1870 on the ruins of an earlier Saadian one. The gardens are part of Marrakech's UNESCO World Heritage listing.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 80 m south-east of the pavilion and basin, and face north-west. The High Atlas mountains are behind you from here, so they won't be in your shot.

card.hook: Picture a marble courtyard the size of 50 by 30 metres, wooden galleries painted in rich colours on every side, and palm trees poking up over the roof. That's the Grand Courtyard at the Bahia Palace, and even a quick snap looks good here.
card.stand_here: Head into the Grand Courtyard (the Cour d'Honneur) and stand close to the central fountain. Face the carved galleries, so the marble and water are at your feet and the palm trees rise behind the building.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the marble floor, fountain and galleries all in one shot. Then try 1x for a more natural look, and 2x or more (depending on your phone) for the painted ceilings and carved details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, keep the fountain low in the frame, let the galleries fill the middle and the palm trees sit at the top, and keep the lines level so the columns stand straight.
card.best_time: Go early, right when it opens, before the tour groups roll in. The courtyards fill up from late morning, and one guide says it gets busier by the minute after opening.
card.selfie_here: Stand close to the central fountain in the Grand Courtyard, use the front camera at 0.5x, and hold it so the palace and the palm trees sit behind your shoulder. For a second one, walk out through the door into the gardens, turn around, and let the carved doorway frame you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand near the central fountain in the Grand Courtyard so the palace and its palm trees show up behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is permitted throughout the palace, but follow any posted signs and don't block passageways while you line up your shot. One guide warns of uneven surfaces and small steps, so watch your feet.
card.challenge: Find a carved, painted doorway and shoot back through it toward the interior, so the doorway becomes your picture frame.
card.good_to_know: The Bahia Palace was begun in the 1860s by the grand vizier Si Musa, and his son Si Ba Ahmed enlarged it between 1894 and 1900. It has around 150 rooms around a string of courtyards and garden courts. The name means "the Brilliant", reportedly after Ba Ahmed's favourite wife.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head into the Grand Courtyard (the Cour d'Honneur) and stand close to the central fountain. Face the carved galleries, so the marble and water are at your feet and the palm trees rise behind the building.

selfie_spots.why: The doorway acts as a natural frame for a shot of you with the palace behind, and the same guide calls the garden paths some of its favourite shots.

card.hook: Picture a palace so grand it was named "the Incomparable", and now it's mostly tall earthen walls, orange trees and storks nesting up top. Somehow that's even better for photos.
card.stand_here: Climb to the top of the eastern rampart, on the eastern side of El Badi Palace and away from the phone icon. Face out over the orange trees and the courtyard.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to catch the whole sweep of gardens, courtyard and walls. Then try 2x to 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) for the storks, or for the Koutoubia minaret if it's showing. Zoom 1x suits the view from courtyard level.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the walls, then slide the brightness a touch darker so the sky keeps its colour and the storks stay crisp.
card.best_time: Late afternoon, when the sun lights up the walls and the storks turn into neat silhouettes. The Koutoubia minaret only shows on clear days, so check when you get there.
card.selfie_here: Stand at the edge of the central pool in the main courtyard, with the walls rising behind you. On a still day they mirror in the water. Or head into the sunken orange gardens at golden hour, when warm light pools at the foot of the walls. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the walls over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: You need an entry ticket for the rampart view, so check the official site for prices and opening times. Drones are generally not permitted. Keep a respectful distance from the storks and never disturb them. There's little shade, so bring a hat, sunscreen and water, and check any signs at the entrance for posted rules.
card.challenge: Take one stork-on-clear-sky shot, and see if you can wait out the bird that keeps flapping off just as you tap.
card.good_to_know: Sultan Ahmad al-Mansur commissioned El Badi in 1578 to receive guests and show off his wealth, with materials brought from as far apart as Italy and Mali. After he died in 1603 it was neglected, and its marble and fittings were stripped out and reused elsewhere in Morocco. The pool isn't always filled, and event structures or scaffolding sometimes block part of the courtyard.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Climb to the top of the eastern rampart, on the eastern side of El Badi Palace and away from the phone icon. Face out over the orange trees and the courtyard.

card.hook: You step out of the kasbah and into a calm green garden, with some of the most richly decorated rooms in Marrakech right beside it. Your phone won't know where to look first.
card.stand_here: Stand in the open garden space between the two buildings, right where the phone icon sits at the heart of the complex. Face the tomb buildings, then walk over to a doorway to peek into the chambers.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x for the garden and the bigger chambers, and 1x for most everyday shots. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for carved and painted details you can't get close to.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of a wall, then slide it a little darker so the decoration keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Go early or late in the day, when it's quieter and the midday sun isn't harsh. Check the official site for visiting times before you set off.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie in the garden courtyard among the lesser tombs, near the Rose Garden graves, with the tomb buildings behind you (morning light filters through here). Or try the doorway arch into the Chamber of the Twelve Columns: use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the arch over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: No flash inside the tombs, as it protects the decorations. Please skip group selfies that could disturb other visitors. Watch your step, as there are uneven surfaces and steps.
card.challenge: Find one repeating pattern, line it up with the gridlines, and see if you can make it dead straight.
card.good_to_know: The Saadian Tombs are a royal burial ground just behind the Kasbah Mosque. Most of what you see dates from the Saadian dynasty, especially the reign of Ahmad al-Mansur (1578-1603). He was buried in the centre of the Twelve Columns chamber in 1603, and many art historians see the complex as the high point of Moroccan architecture of that period.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the open garden space between the two buildings, right where the phone icon sits at the heart of the complex. Face the tomb buildings, then walk over to a doorway to peek into the chambers.

Sources conflict on interior photography: one page says photography inside the tombs is not allowed, while several others allow it without flash. Opening hours also differ between sources (9:00 to 17:00 on some pages, 8:30–11:45 and 14:30–17:45 on another), so check before going. No page mentions selfie sticks or tripod rules. The entrance is unmarked on Rue de la Kasbah, just past the Kasbah Mosque.

card.hook: The Kutubiyya minaret is 77 metres tall, and you can't go inside, so the best show is from the gardens at its feet. Palms, orange trees and roses do the framing for you.
card.stand_here: Walk into Koutoubia Gardens on the south side of the mosque. It's about 200 metres west of Jemaa el-Fnaa, roughly 3 minutes on foot. Face north and the minaret is right there.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole tower with the trees around it. Try 0.5x if you want a pool or flower bed in front, but keep the tower in the middle. Zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) gets you the decorated top and spire.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the tower up with a vertical line, and keep your phone upright so it fills the screen height.
card.best_time: Go at sunrise or sunset, when the stone turns gold or ochre. Sunset is the popular pick, while sunrise is likely to have fewer people.
card.selfie_here: Stand under the arch to the left of the main entrance, use the front camera and look up so the minaret sits over your shoulder. For a watery version, stand at the edge of the long, narrow reflecting pool by the garden fountain, with the tower rising above the water behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the south-side garden paths, a short distance back from the mosque, so the whole minaret fits with orange trees and palms in front.
card.rules_and_safety: Non-Muslims can't go into the mosque or minaret, so every photo is taken from outside. Exterior photos are fine, but avoid photographing worshippers, especially during prayer. One review mentions construction work near the archway and old prayer hall ruins, so check when you arrive.
card.challenge: Take three shots from three slightly different spots and see which one the palms don't photobomb.
card.good_to_know: The mosque was founded in 1147 and rebuilt around 1158, and the minaret was probably finished around 1195. The name means 'booksellers', after the book trade that once filled the streets around its base. It's the largest mosque in Marrakech and a symbol of the city.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk into Koutoubia Gardens on the south side of the mosque. It's about 200 metres west of Jemaa el-Fnaa, roughly 3 minutes on foot. Face north and the minaret is right there.

card.hook: The whole front of this museum looks like woven fabric, but it's made of bricks. Everyone who walks up wants the same photo of the big YSL letters, so expect a friendly queue.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject, in front of the entrance with the large YSL lettering, and face the letters so the façade fills the frame behind them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the entrance and the logo. Try zoom 2x to get close to the brick lattice, where the pattern looks even better.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, line the lettering up with one of them, and keep your phone level so the brick lines stay straight.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or near closing time, when the queue at the logo is shorter.
card.selfie_here: Take it at the big metal YSL logo on the courtyard wall, after you've bought your ticket and before you go inside. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze more in, and keep the logo over your shoulder. The queue there is long, so have your pose ready.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the far side of Rue Yves Saint Laurent, opposite the museum sign where traffic is light, while you stand with the museum entrance behind you. Check the framing, because we can't promise the whole building fits.
card.rules_and_safety: Photo rules differ between accounts. One says no photos inside the museum, another says photos are fine everywhere except the main exhibition hall, so check on arrival. Keep clear of the cacti outside, because one photo shoot there ended badly for a tulle skirt.
card.challenge: Take one close-up of the brick lattice and one wide shot from the street, then see which one your friends like better.
card.good_to_know: The museum opened on 19 October 2017 and covers 4,000 square metres. Studio KO designed it, and the bricks were made locally from Moroccan earth. In 2018 it won Wallpaper magazine's award for best new public building.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the subject, in front of the entrance with the large YSL lettering, and face the letters so the façade fills the frame behind them.

card.hook: Picture a wall that's built like a layer cake: tiles at the bottom, calligraphy at eye level, carved stucco above, then carved wooden eaves on top. That's the courtyard at Ben Youssef Madrasa, and it's even better with a pool in the middle.
card.stand_here: Head to the Ben Youssef Madrasa, right next to the Ben Youssef Mosque. The phone icon on the map sits at the building itself. Stand at the edge of the courtyard near the pool and face along its length, so the galleries run evenly down both sides.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the pool and the galleries into one frame, because the courtyard is tight. Switch to 1x for calmer, less stretched arches, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the tilework, carved stucco and entrance vault.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the middle of the pool up with the middle of the frame, then tap the walls and slide it a touch darker so the bright sky doesn't wash out the carving.
card.best_time: Early in the day is likely to be quieter, which is handy for clean shots of the courtyard. Later, when the sun is higher, light reaches further in, but the contrast between sunny and shaded walls can be strong.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the far side of the reflecting pool, so the courtyard arches are right behind you, and use the front camera at 0.5x if your phone has it. Or take one just outside the entrance, on the two street-side arches, with the madrasa's facade over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a friendly passer-by, stand at the pool yourself, and ask them to shoot from the centre of the courtyard straight along the pool, then shift so the pool runs sideways across the frame and all five arches fit in.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos without flash are fine throughout the madrasa. Check the official site before you go for current access arrangements.
card.challenge: Find the spot where the pool gives you a soft reflection of the arches, then crouch low with your phone close to the water and see how good you can make it.
card.good_to_know: The madrasa was finished in 1564-65 under the Saadian sultan Abdallah al-Ghalib and is named after the neighbouring Ben Youssef Mosque. At its height it was the largest madrasa in the Maghreb, with 130 student rooms and space for up to 800 students. It closed in 1960, reopened as a historical site in 1982, and reopened again in April 2022 after a restoration that began in November 2018.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the Ben Youssef Madrasa, right next to the Ben Youssef Mosque. The phone icon on the map sits at the building itself. Stand at the edge of the courtyard near the pool and face along its length, so the galleries run evenly down both sides.

card.hook: Here's the twist: the best-known photo of the Ben Youssef Mosque area doesn't have the mosque in it. High walls hide most of the mosque from the street, so the postcard view is taken next door in the madrasa courtyard.
card.stand_here: Stand in the central courtyard of the Ben Youssef Madrasa, on the far side of the reflecting pool from the arches, and face the arches. The mosque itself is about 95 m to the west of the madrasa.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x, which is right for the courtyard. If the arches get cut off at the sides, switch to 0.5x and keep your phone level so the lines don't lean. Zoom 2x to 5x is good for carved details, or for the minaret when you can see it between the walls (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, put the pool's edge on a lower line with the arches centred, and crouch so you catch more reflection.
card.best_time: Go right at opening, when the pool is calm and the courtyard is empty. Take a second shot a moment later in case ripples spoil the reflection.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and stand in front of the two arches just outside the madrasa entrance, with the carved doorway behind you. Visitors say these are among the most photographed backdrops at the site. Switch to 0.5x if you want more of the arches in the frame.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the far side of the pool in front of the arches, and ask your helper to stand where the pool runs horizontally in front of them, so all five arches fit with some pool in the foreground.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are allowed indoors in public areas, but skip the flash in delicate areas and follow any signs that restrict photos. Be discreet around worshippers and other visitors, and ask before photographing people. The mosque itself isn't open to non-Muslim visitors, and the madrasa courtyard is ticketed, so check current ticket details first (one guide notes entry is cash only).
card.challenge: Take the same reflection shot twice, once with the pool rippling and once still as glass, and see which one you'd put on a postcard.
card.good_to_know: The mosque is named after the Almoravid ruler Ali ibn Yusuf, who built a grand central mosque here, completed between 1120 and 1132. The building you see today is a rebuild finished in 1819-20, with a minaret of around 40 metres. The madrasa next door, just to the east, was founded in 1563-64 as a theological college.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the central courtyard of the Ben Youssef Madrasa, on the far side of the reflecting pool from the arches, and face the arches. The mosque itself is about 95 m to the west of the madrasa.

card.hook: Step into the courtyard and your neck does the work first: a huge brass chandelier, cut into geometric and arabesque patterns, hangs right above the fountains. Colourful tiles and carved cedar wood surround it on every side.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, inside the central courtyard of the Marrakech Museum. Face the middle of the courtyard so the fountains are in front of you and the chandelier is above them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole courtyard in. Then go to 1x for calmer, less stretched views of the fountains and galleries. Try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for close-ups of the tilework or the chandelier.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, line the chandelier up with the centre of the courtyard, and keep your phone level so the gallery lines don't lean.
card.best_time: The courtyard is roofed over, so the light stays soft and even and the time of day matters less than it would outdoors. Pick a moment when it's less crowded so you get clear shots without strangers in the frame.
card.selfie_here: Stand in the middle of the courtyard, under the chandelier by the central fountain, which is the classic shot here. Use the front camera, hold it a little low and tilt up so the chandelier and tiles sit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the entrance archway and frame the whole courtyard, while you stand inside it by the fountains.
card.rules_and_safety: Rules on photography inside, and on entry, can change, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one perfectly symmetrical shot of the chandelier, then one where a tiled arch frames it from the side. Which one wins?
card.good_to_know: The museum is inside the Dar Mnebhi Palace, built at the start of the 20th century by Mehdi al-Mnebhi, a minister of war under Sultan Moulay Abdelaziz. It later became a girls' school, then was carefully restored and opened as a museum in 1997. There's also a hammam with domed, vaulted chambers, plus carpets, costumes, pottery and Berber jewellery for easy close-ups.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, inside the central courtyard of the Marrakech Museum. Face the middle of the courtyard so the fountains are in front of you and the chandelier is above them.

card.hook: Look at Bab Agnaou and you'll notice something odd: the carved frame is way bigger than the doorway under it. Someone later tucked a smaller, plainer brick arch inside, and the old carving got to keep the spotlight.
card.stand_here: Stand on Rue de la Kasbah, on the Kasbah side, just inside the gate. Turn around and face back toward the carved façade, with the Kasbah streets leading away behind you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to catch the gate and the street. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the carved bands and the lettering without stepping near the traffic. Use 0.5x only if the street is quiet.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the middle of the arch with the centre of the screen so the symmetry really shows.
card.best_time: Golden hour is your best bet, because the sandstone glows warm in low sun. Midday is the busiest and trickiest time, with crowds and traffic in every shot.
card.selfie_here: Try the inner-medina side of the arch: use the front camera and stand with the carved gate behind you. Switch to 0.5x to fit more of the arch in, and take a few frames so one is free of strangers.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across the wide road, or on the median strip, facing the gate while you stand by the arch, and suggest they zoom in slightly to cut out the traffic.
card.rules_and_safety: Traffic on the wide road in front of the gate is fast and chaotic, so stick to the pavement or the median and never stand in the road for a photo.
card.challenge: Spot the little carved shells hiding in the floral corners of the arch, and get one in your photo.
card.good_to_know: Bab Agnaou was the main public entrance to the royal Kasbah. Its construction is attributed to the Almohad caliph Abu Yusuf Ya'qub al-Mansur, and it was finished around 1188 or 1190. The flanking towers are gone, and a band of Quranic lettering still frames the whole façade.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Rue de la Kasbah, on the Kasbah side, just inside the gate. Turn around and face back toward the carved façade, with the Kasbah streets leading away behind you.

card.hook: Most people photograph the big arch and walk off, but the mosque right beside it is where the quieter picture is. The gate sits on a busy corner of the medina, with buses and bustle just outside, and the minaret rises calmly above it all.
card.stand_here: Stand at Bab Doukkala, on the north-western edge of the Marrakech medina, where the phone icon on the map sits right at the gate. Turn to face the neighbouring mosque and shoot its entrance and minaret from outside.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the mosque doorway. Go to 2x or 5x for the minaret and its details (higher zooms depend on your phone). Use 0.5x only when you want the whole gate and the square in one shot.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and keep the minaret on one vertical line so it doesn't lean, then tap the minaret and slide darker a touch so the sky stays blue.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives you softer light and fewer people and vehicles around the bus area.
card.selfie_here: Try the small rise just outside the gate, then turn back toward the arch and the ramparts. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the gate over your shoulder. One local blog suggests dawn there, but it's a viewpoint to test, so see what works for you.
card.rules_and_safety: The mosque is a place of worship, so photograph it from outside and be discreet around people at prayer. Ask before taking close-ups of people, especially vendors. It's a busy area, so keep an eye on the roads, stay aware of your surroundings and keep your valuables secure.
card.challenge: Take one picture where the minaret is perfectly straight against the sky, with a sliver of doorway at the bottom to show how big it is.
card.good_to_know: The gate dates back to around 1126, when the Almoravid emir Ali ibn Yusuf built the city's first walls. It still has its original bent entrance, where the passage turns at a right angle twice (west, then south, then east) before it reaches the city. The mosque beside it is Saadian-era, so it's much younger than the gate.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at Bab Doukkala, on the north-western edge of the Marrakech medina, where the phone icon on the map sits right at the gate. Turn to face the neighbouring mosque and shoot its entrance and minaret from outside.

card.hook: Most palaces make you look straight ahead, but Dar Si Said makes you look up too, because it's built over more than one level. Painted wood, patterned surfaces and a garden pavilion are all packed into one stop.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, at Dar Si Said itself, so the palace and garden are all around you. Face the building and garden side on and get your main shot first, then wander.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the building and the garden pavilion. Drop to 0.5x in tight rooms or the courtyard, and try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for carved wood, painted ceilings and tile patterns.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the scene, then slide the brightness down a touch so the painted and carved surfaces keep their rich colour.
card.best_time: Go when the museum is open, and check the official site first because access has varied since the 2023 earthquake. The main courtyard is often less crowded than other Marrakech sights, so aim for a quiet moment.
card.selfie_here: Take it in the central courtyard of the museum, with the tilework and greenery behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x and tilt it slightly up so the ornament fills the space over your shoulder. For fewer people in the background, try the smaller secondary courtyards.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally allowed in public areas and courtyards, but skip the flash, and follow any signs or staff instructions. Be respectful of local residents' privacy when you photograph around the city. The selfie spots are inside the museum, which needs a ticket.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of a room, then find a single carved or painted detail in it and fill the whole screen with it.
card.good_to_know: Dar Si Said was built between 1894 and 1900 for Si Sa'id ibn Musa, a vizier and minister of defence. Today it's the National Museum of Weaving and Carpets, reopened in 2018 after renovation. It was badly damaged in the September 2023 earthquake and closed for repairs, so how much you can see inside may vary.
